messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Rstan: naming, system, etc.
parts:
1. Naming

I'm with Andrew that we should call the package:

Stan

Though I like caps.

That confuses the code organization a bit now, as
we have a directory:

stan/rstan/rstan

with all of the R stuff in it. How about changing
the name of that to:

stan/R/stan

?

2. I'm looking at the stan.R code that Ben inserted.
It uses a system() call. Is this going to work cross
platform? That's where I was imagining we'd have a
compile command implemented through Rcpp so that the
compiler ran in the same process as R itself.

If we do a system call, we need to worry about supplying
an executable or having users compile the code.

Given our problems with Windows compilers, this may turn
out to be easier than compiling through R(cpp).

I don't understand the design decisions well enough here.


3. Is inline related to Rcpp in any way other than having
the same author? I did find this blog of John Cook's:

http://www.johndcook.com/blog/2011/06/30/calling-cpp-from-r/

- Bob

On Feb 28, 3:49 pm, Bob Carpenter <c...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> 1.  Naming
>
> I'm with Andrew that we should call the package:
>
>     Stan
>
> Though I like caps.
>
> That confuses the code organization a bit now, as
> we have a directory:
>
>     stan/rstan/rstan
>
> with all of the R stuff in it.  How about changing
> the name of that to:
>
>     stan/R/stan
>
> ?

That is okay, although has the confusion that a directory will be stan/
R/stan/R/ .

But I am not sure we should change the name of the R package to stan.
The dominant naming convention for R packages that interface with
external software is to have R or R2 or something in the name
(R2WinBUGS, RcppEigen, etc.). If you ever intend to have them packaged
for Linux distributions, having two source packages with the same name
will cause some headaches. Finally, since stan the library is BSD and
stan the R package is GPL, I'd say that having distinct names would be
less legally confusing.

> 2.  I'm looking at the stan.R code that Ben inserted.
> It uses a system() call.  Is this going to work cross
> platform?  That's where I was imagining we'd have a
> compile command implemented through Rcpp so that the
> compiler ran in the same process as R itself.

Yes. Nowdays there is system2() which is more portable in a sense but
was only introduced into R a couple of years ago.

> If we do a system call, we need to worry about supplying
> an executable or having users compile the code.

Executable what exactly? Executables like demo/gm should exist once
the user installs the R package (whether they build it from source or
install the binary R package). For executables like particular models,
then the user would have to compile them, in which case on Windows
they need the Rtools toolchain (not VisualStudio).

> 3.  Is inline related to Rcpp in any way other than having
> the same author?  I did find this blog of John Cook's:

Most of the code in the inline package was originally written by Oleg
Sklyar. The inline package is a suggestency of the Rcpp package
because some R functions in Rcpp utilize inline.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Rstan: naming, system, etc.
parts:
OK, this would probably be easier if I just came to the stan meeting. When is that?

What I had in my head was that the R package would have an inst/include/ directory that basically contained stan/src/. When the R package gets installed (from source), the installation would essentially involve a "make demo/gm". That is essentially what the RcppEigen package does. The binary version of the R package (built from source by / on CRAN's servers) would thus have the demo/gm executable.

Once the R package is installed and loaded, the main stan() function would use the system() or system2() function to pass a .stan text file to demo/gm to yield the C++ file, which would then get processed by Rcpp's magic. Then, the main stan() function would use the .Call() function in R to pass the data to the just-compiled model and execute.

But there are probably other ways to do it as well.

Ben
